cases.statement: Review this Rust function for bugs: `fn increment(x: u8) -> u8 { x + 1 }`. Cite sources from the list.

checks.label: notes the debug panic or a test for the edge

sources.title: Rust std: u8::checked_add
sources.excerpt: checked_add returns None on overflow instead of wrapping or panicking.

sources.title: TRPL: integer types
sources.excerpt: Integer overflow panics in debug builds and wraps in release builds.

agent_a.text: Yes: `x + 1` overflows for x=255 (wraps in release, panics in debug). Use `u8::checked_add` and test the edge. See CITE[1] and CITE[2].

agent_b.text: The function looks fine; it just adds one.

critique.text: The review is right about overflow at 255 and the checked_add fix; also cite the TRPL chapter on debug panics.

revision.text: Yes: `x + 1` overflows at x=255 — wraps in release, panics in debug. Use checked_add and add a unit test for 255. CITE[1] CITE[2]

synthesis.text: The function overflows for x=255; use checked_add and test the edge. CITE[1]

cases.statement: Review this Rust function for bugs: `fn average(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { (a + b) / 2 }`. Cite sources from the list.

sources.title: Rust std: i32 overflow behaviour
sources.excerpt: In debug builds, overflowing arithmetic panics; release builds wrap.

sources.title: A guide to defensive integer arithmetic
sources.excerpt: Prefer widening or checked operations when inputs can reach the type's bounds.

agent_a.text: Yes: a + b can overflow for large inputs. Add tests for extreme values.

agent_b.text: The average is correct; division handles everything.

critique.text: The review misses the fix: widen to i64 or use i32::checked_add before dividing, and test the boundary values.

revision.text: Yes: a + b can overflow — widen to i64 or use i32::checked_add, and test the boundary values. CITE[2]

synthesis.text: The sum can overflow; widen to i64 or use checked_add, and test the boundaries. CITE[1]

cases.statement: Should an engineering org ban all AI-generated code that has not been human-reviewed? Cite sources from the list.

sources.title: 2025 State of AI code review (excerpt)
sources.excerpt: Teams report that blanket manual review gates cut delivery velocity on low-risk changes.

sources.title: Org policy template: risk tiers
sources.excerpt: High-risk changes require approval; low-risk changes may use lighter gates.

agent_a.text: A blanket ban ignores context: low-risk generated code could move faster with human review on a risk-tiered basis; higher-risk changes need approval. Productivity suffers if everything is gated equally. CITE[1] CITE[2]

agent_b.text: Yes, ban it all: generated code is unsafe.

critique.text: The answer lacks the productivity dimension and a tiering mechanism — the decision depends on risk context, not a blanket rule.

revision.text: Propose risk tiers: auto-approve low-risk changes with mandatory human review for high-risk ones, and track velocity impact — the right rule depends on context. CITE[1] CITE[2]

synthesis.text: Banning everything is blunt: the decision depends on risk context. Require human review for high-risk changes, allow a fast path for low-risk ones, and measure the velocity impact. CITE[1]

cases.statement: Should the project auto-merge dependency updates whenever CI passes? Cite sources from the list.

sources.title: Supply-chain attack report 2025 (excerpt)
sources.excerpt: Most compromised packages passed automated CI; the attack was in the code, not the build.

sources.title: CI trust levels guide
sources.excerpt: Reserve auto-merge for low-risk, signature-verified updates.

agent_a.text: Yes, auto-merge everything that passes CI — CI passing means it works.

agent_b.text: No blanket rule: dependencies are a supply-chain risk. Auto-merge only low-risk updates with verified signatures; keep human review for critical ones — the decision depends on the risk tier. CITE[1] CITE[2]

critique.text: The answer ignores supply-chain risk: compromised packages pass CI. The rule must depend on the risk tier, not on CI alone.

revision.text: Auto-merge only low-risk updates with verified signatures and CI; require human review for critical dependencies — supply-chain attacks make a blanket rule dangerous. CITE[1] CITE[2]

synthesis.text: Use a tiered rule: auto-merge verified low-risk updates, human review for critical ones — CI alone does not catch supply-chain attacks. CITE[1] CITE[2]
